claims.assertion: This was a RydeTAXI trip billed by the meter for 22.32 km (F7), so the +2.5 km of extra driving over the 19.8 km optimal route (F1) passed straight into the fare; the metered structure is why a route deviation is refundable here at all.

GPS records one off-route segment 09:53–10:01 in which 4.49 km were driven where the optimal route covers 2.33 km, adding 2.15 km and taking the car up to 1009 m off the optimal route (F3); this is an un-exempted detour segment unless an exemption applies.

The driver's own pre-departure message at 09:50 asked about a route via Bedok North Avenue 3 (F8) and the rider's reply at 09:50 — '可以，走 Bedok North Avenue 3 吧' (F9) — is a specific named-road authorisation limited to driving on Bedok North Avenue 3, not a general 'take whatever route is faster' licence.

No fact in the record ties the driven off-route segment (F3, 09:53–10:01, up to 1009 m off route) to Bedok North Avenue 3: the chat contains no location on that road during the segment and there is no road-name fact, so the correspondence required by RD-5 is absent and that segment is at most undetermined for consent purposes.

The deviation is not justified by traffic: no traffic incidents were recorded near the route in the trip window (F14), and the only congestion record is a speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) on Pan Island Expressway during 09:27–09:53 (F12), which is at most corroborative under RD-4(b) and there is no RD-4(a) incident covering the replaced part of the optimal route; weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain (F15).

Traffic on the corridor does not explain the 9.9 minutes and 2.5 km over estimate (F1, F2), since the airport-side segment on Airport Boulevard was running at band 5, 40–49 km/h (F13); the segment therefore falls to RD-2 as un-exempted.
The refund on the un-exempted segment is 2.15 km × this trip's per-km rate of $1.4099, i.e. $3.03, rounded to the cent; the rider's own fare figures supply both the extra km and the per-km rate (F4).

Waiting of only 0.4 min was billed at $0.11 (F5) — a metered waiting unit on a RydeTAXI trip, which is not refundable under RD-3(c) — and no other un-disclosed add-on appears in the breakdown, so the route is the only disputed item (F7).

The driver has 2 route disputes upheld in the last 90 days (F17); since this case makes the deviation refund positive, the rider asks for the account-review flag as an additional action (F16 shows the rider's own clean record).

weaknesses: The rider did send an approving message ('可以，走 Bedok North Avenue 3 吧', F9) before the segment began, so the driver will argue RD-5 consent covers the whole diversion; the honest weakness is that the rider cannot show the car was in fact off Bedok North Avenue 3, and under RD-5/G13 the judge may find the segment undetermined rather than un-exempted, which sends at least part of the question to a human reviewer.

The rider's complaint itself concedes she agreed to a change of road, and no fact records the road name actually driven, so the driver's post-trip statement (F11) that the rider agreed will be used against us — though a statement is not consent under RD-5 at most it supports the argument that the general intent to reroute existed.

GPS does place the car up to 1009 m off the optimal route with 4.49 km driven where 2.33 km was optimal (F3), but the segment's 2.15 km excess is only $3.03 at the metered rate (F4), so the claim is small; the lump-sum overage the rider perceives (F7) is mostly the ordinary metered distance/time for the whole trip and is not recoverable.

Traffic shows band 2 congestion on PIE during 09:27–09:53 (F12), which the driver will cite as a reasonable cause for rerouting a taxi trip; it is only corroborative under RD-4(b), but a judge may treat it as explaining part of the deviation.

claims.assertion: The rider expressly agreed to the named route in a message sent before the off-route segment began: F8 (driver asks at 09:50 whether he may go via Bedok North Avenue 3) is followed by F9 (rider, 09:50: “可以，走 Bedok North Avenue 3吧。”), and the only off-route segment starts at 09:53 (F3), so consent preceded the segment by three minutes.

The record is complete and every message is timestamped (F10), so the RD-5 'before you go' timing test can be applied to this consent without any G12 gap; the rider's consent is her own in-app message (F9), not merely the driver's assertion in F11.

Real congestion on the replaced optimal route gives a reasonable cause for the reroute: the optimal route's Pan Island Expressway was in speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) throughout 09:27–09:53 (F12), matching the window in which the driver proposed the alternative at 09:50 (F8) and the start of the off-route segment at 09:53 (F3); F14 shows no incident record but does not contradict the congestion evidence.

Because the rider named a specific road (F9) and the reroute was proposed and accepted before the segment for exactly that congestion reason (F8, F12), the whole of the single off-route segment 09:53–10:01 (F3, +2.15 km) falls within the agreed, justified route change and no part of it is an unexempted detour.

The billed distance-based excess of $3.52 (2.50 km × $1.4099/km, F4) corresponds to the same 2.5 km global excess measured by GPS (F1) and to the 2.15 km segment in F3, so the sum the rider says is 'much more expensive than the estimate' is a metered, per-Kilometre amount owed for distance actually driven, not an unauthorised extra charge.

All other charged items are published, meter-based items: waiting $0.11 for 0.4 min (F5) is a metered waiting unit, and the total $46.40 (F7) contains only base $3.90, distance $31.47, time $9.45, waiting $0.11 and platform $1.47 with no surge (F6) and no unpublished add-on, so there is nothing to refund under the fare rules.

The trip was longer in time as well as distance (36.8 min actual vs 26.9 min estimated, +9.9 min, F2), which is consistent with the congestion documented on the expressway in F12 rather than with the driver taking a deliberately slow or aimless detour.

No safety event applies: the chat contains only a route request and a route agreement (F8, F9) with no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, and the driver's statement is likewise innocuous (F11), so the case should be decided under the route-deviation rules and not escalated.

weaknesses: F9 consents only to 'driving on Bedok North Avenue 3' (a named-road authorisation), and the index contains no fact that ties the driven segment itself to that road (no road-name fact, no locating message): on RD-5's named-road limb with G13 in mind, the judge may find the scope of consent undetermined for the 09:53–10:01 segment rather than fully agreed.

The GPS excess is not fully accounted for by the agreed segment: total excess is +2.5 km (F1) while the segment adds only 2.15 km (F3), so the rider will argue the remaining mileage and the +9.9 min duration (F2) are unexplained distance on the agreed route.

RD-4(a) is not satisfied: there is no traffic incident record at all (F14), and under RD-4(b)/G3 the band 2 record in F12 is, on its own, only corroborative and not a stand-alone exemption — so the driver must rely on the rider's consent, not on 'reasonable cause' alone.
The driver's own written statement in F11 is merely a self-serving assertion of verbal consent; if the judge treats the consent as resting on F11 rather than F9, G11 says it counts for nothing.
Profile F17 (2 route disputes upheld in the last 90 days) gives the rider a ready RD-6 hook: if even one unexempted kilometre is found, the driver risks a flag_account referral on this trip's record.

points.response: Timing alone is not consent: RD-5 requires the agreed message to cover the segment actually driven, and here nothing ties the 09:53–10:01 segment (F3, up to 1009 m off the optimal route) to Bedok North Avenue 3 — there is no road-name fact and no locating message — so the segment that F3 describes is not the segment F9 authorises.

Agreed — F10 shows two timestamped messages and F9 is the rider's own message, so the G11/G12 objections do not bite; but completeness of the record does not supply the RD-5 correspondence between the agreed road and the driven segment, which is what G13 requires.

The one traffic fact on the optimal route is band 2 on PIE during 09:27–09:53 (F12) while F14 records no incident at all, and by RD-4(b) with G3 a band record alone is only corroborative; note also that F12's window ends at 09:53, exactly when the segment starts (F3), so it does not cover the segment that actually added the km.

This is the crux and it fails: RD-5 limits a named-road authorisation to driving on that road, and with no record linking the driven segment to Bedok North Avenue 3 the judge is to find the segment undetermined rather than exempt (G13); RD-4(a) is unavailable because F14 shows no incident, so the 2.15 km of F3 is un-exempted under RD-2.

RD-2 refunds exactly this metre-measured excess: 2.15 km (F3) at this trip's per-km rate of $1.4099 (F4) = $3.03; the driver's own figure of $3.52 for 2.50 km (F4) confirms the excess distance was billed as distance, which is why it must come back when the segment is un-exempted.

Conceded as to items other than mileage — the $0.11 metered waiting unit (F5) and the published components in F7 with no surge (F6) are not refundable — so my claim is limited to the $3.03 mileage on the un-exempted segment.

Duration cuts the other way after 09:53: with no incident (F14) and PIE's band 2 window ending at 09:53 (F12), the +9.9 min (F2) sits inside the off-route segment (F3) and on the airport corridor running at band 5, 40–49 km/h (F13) — congestion cannot carry the +9.9 minutes.
Agreed, no safety escalation: F8, F9 and F11 contain no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving content, so SAFE-1/SAFE-2 are not engaged and the case is decided on route and fare rules.

I maintain the flag request: RD-6 attaches once the RD-2 refund is positive, and F17 shows 2 route disputes upheld in the last 90 days, making this case the repeat; F4 supplies the positive amount ($3.03).

Accepted as far as it goes: on a metered RydeTAXI trip distance is billed (F7), but that only means RD-2 is the right vehicle for the arithmetic — it does not establish that any segment is unexempted, which is the point the rider concedes nothing on.

The single segment in F3 is not automatically unexempted; RD-1 sends every segment through RD-3/RD-4/RD-5, and here the rider's own message in F9 agreed to the route change three minutes before the segment began at 09:53 (F8, F3).

Correct that F9 is a named-road authorisation, but the driver asked for that exact road for the stated reason that traffic on the expressway was building up (F8), and the expressway was in fact in speed band 2 at 10–19 km/h during 09:27–09:53 (F12), so the agreement was an informed route choice, not a licence the driver exceeded.

The rider is right that no fact in the record names the road actually driven, so on RD-5's named-road limb the judge may treat the segment as undetermined rather than agreed; the driver does not claim a fact that does not exist, and asks only that the benefit of the doubt not be turned into an affirmative finding of an unexcused detour.

The rider's own cited fact confirms the congestion rather than denying it: F12 records the optimal route's Pan Island Expressway at band 2 (10–19 km/h) covering 09:27–09:53, which is exactly why the driver asked to divert at 09:50 (F8) and drove the alternative from 09:53 (F3); F14's absence of an incident record and the fair weather in F15 do not disprove that congestion.

F13 only shows the airport-side road running freely at the end of the trip; it says nothing about the expressway stretch at 09:27–09:53, and the +9.9 min in F2 is consistent with the driver having driven 4.49 km in eight minutes on the substituted segment (F3) while the original corridor was congested (F12).

The $3.03 figure is arithmetically available on the rider's own numbers (2.15 km × $1.4099, F3, F4), but it is only payable if a segment is unexempted, and the driver's position is that the agreed, congestion-motivated segment is exempt under RD-5/RD-4, so the correct amount is nil.

Agreed, and it cuts for the driver: the rider concedes the only disputed item is the route, the metered waiting unit of $0.11 for 0.4 min (F5) is not refundable, and the $46.40 total (F7) contains no surge (F6) and no unpublished add-on.

RD-6 requires a refund greater than zero or a recorded RD-1 breach in this case before the flag can attach, and here there is none; the rider's own message in F9 agreeing to the exact road at issue (F8) is what defeats the predicate, so the 90-day profile in F17 cannot be used to manufacture it.
